title: kitty SIGBUS: non-atomic PNG writes truncate assets kitty has mmap'd
description:
kitty 0.48.2 crashed 2026-08-26 16:52 EDT with SIGBUS while decoding one of our PNGs.
Crash report: kitty-crash-report-2026-08-1600EDT.txt (repo root, untracked).

EVIDENCE
  Exception:  EXC_BAD_ACCESS (SIGBUS), KERN_MEMORY_ERROR at 0x1186bc029
  Region:     "mapped file" 1186bc000-1186c0000 [16K] r--/r-- (fault 41 bytes in)
  Triage:     CL   - cluster_pagein past EOF
              APFS - cluster_pagein() failed
              VM   - Filesystem pagein returned an error in vnode_pagein
  Stack:      main thread -> kitty.fast_data_types -> png_read_image ->
              png_read_row -> _platform_memmove  (crash frame)

"cluster_pagein past EOF" with a fault only 41 bytes into the mapping means the
file got SHORTER than the mapping while libpng was reading rows out of it - i.e.
truncated to ~0 underneath kitty. Not a decode bug, not bad PNG data.

MECHANISM
1. zsh/prompt_lcars.zsh:114-122 (_lc_transmit) transmits with t=f - kitty is
   handed a PATH (base64'd) and reads/mmaps the file ASYNCHRONOUSLY, on its own
   schedule. The function's own comment says so. Paths point at
   _LCARS_DIR (line 14), the deployed kitty/lcars asset directory.
2. deploy.sh:70 copies into that exact directory with a plain in-place copy,
   which opens the destination O_TRUNC: the file is 0 bytes for the duration of
   the copy. AGENTS.md tells us to run ./deploy.sh after EVERY edit.
3. generate/gen_swoops.py:144,166,205 call img.save(path) - PIL also truncates
   in place. Same hazard for the nvim cache asset dir, whose files
   image_registry hands to image.nvim by path.

So: deploy (or regenerate assets) while any kitty window is drawing an LCARS
prompt, and kitty can be mid-png_read_image on a file just truncated under it.

TIMING: commits at 15:05 and 15:16 that afternoon, crash at 16:52 - an active
dev session. mtimes on the deployed 19x38 PNGs were overwritten by later
deploy.sh runs (2026-08-27 10:48), so mtime evidence is gone, but the nvim cache
dir shows no write in the crash window, which rules that path out and leaves the
deployed dir as the exposed one.

FIX OPTIONS (not mutually exclusive)
 A. Atomic writes - write a sibling temp file, then rename(2) (atomic on APFS).
    A rename swaps the directory entry; kitty's existing mapping keeps the old
    inode alive until it closes it, so there is never a window where the mapped
    file is short.
      deploy.sh:70   copy to "$dest.tmp.$$", then mv -f onto "$dest"
      gen_swoops.py  img.save(tmp); os.replace(tmp, path)   x3 sites
    This is the general fix - it also covers the nvim/image.nvim consumer.
 B. Switch _lc_transmit to t=d (inline base64 PNG bytes). kitty never opens the
    file, so there is nothing to race. The comment above the printf already
    describes t=d as the synchronous, race-free choice - it reads as if the code
    once did this and regressed to t=f. Also fixes the "can miss the first
    placeholder draw" problem the same comment describes.

NOTE: that comment and the code disagree today (comment explains t=d; the printf
sends t=f). Worth resolving either way.
notes:
Option A (atomic writes) implemented 2026-08-27. Option B (t=d vs t=f in
_lc_transmit) deliberately NOT done — still open on this bead.

CHANGES
  deploy.sh deploy_one()      copy to "$dest.deploy.$$", cmp the temp, then
                              mv -f onto the destination. All three steps
                              guarded; on any failure the temp is removed and
                              the destination is left untouched.
  gen_swoops.py save_atomic() new helper; the 3 img.save(path) sites now call
                              it. Temp keeps a .png suffix because PIL infers
                              the format from the extension.
  docs/asset-pipeline.md      new "Never rewrite an asset PNG in place" section
                              stating the invariant and why.

VERIFICATION
  - Patched generator vs the pre-patch generator (extracted from git HEAD),
    same args: output byte-for-byte identical. The change is behavior-preserving.
  - 17 assets generated, zero leftover *.tmp.png.
  - deploy.sh: 33 files ok, no FAIL/SKIP, zero leftover *.deploy.* temps.
  - Atomicity proven by inode: destination inode changed across a deploy
    (37499691 -> 37499885), i.e. the file was replaced by rename, not written
    in place. An existing mmap therefore keeps the old inode.
  - Failure path exercised against a read-only destination dir: prints FAIL,
    returns 1, leaves the old destination content intact, no temp left behind.
    (Strictly better than before — the old cp would have left the destination
    truncated.)
  - Runtime cache-miss path checked too: chrome.lua:27 and the zsh prompt shell
    out to the DEPLOYED gen_swoops.py copy; that copy has save_atomic and
    regenerates correctly.

INCIDENTAL FINDING (not addressed, not a regression)
  Regenerating the 19x38 periwinkle set reproduces 11 of the committed
  assets/*.png with identical PIXELS but different bytes — Pillow/zlib version
  drift in the encoder, pre-existing. Only matters if byte-comparing assets.

title: Tab A right cap hidden by bar highlight extmark
description:
Regression introduced by the 2m7.10 attempted fix for right-cap sharp corners. In `nvim/lua/lcars/block_demo.lua:321`, `bar_w = (lp + bw) - bar_x0` extends the LcarsBlockBar extmark across cap_x..cap_x+1 (the two cells where the vcap image sits). The extmark renders at HL_PRI=200 which sits above the image in nvim + image.nvim + kitty, so a solid periwinkle rectangle covers the cap entirely.

## Observed
User: "The caps at the ends of headers and footers is missing, probably a BG color overlay extending past the caps. If I scroll the viewport right, since the caps are fixed position on scroll, I can see them." (Scrolling separates screen-coord images from buffer-coord extmarks — confirms the cause.)

## Affects
All four barrow calls in make_A: header rows h0, h0+1 and footer rows f0+1, f0+2 (block_demo.lua:324-330).

## Constraint
The reverse fix (`bar_w = cap_x - bar_x0`) restores cap visibility but reopens the original 2b "sharp corner" problem: the vcap PNG has transparent outer corners, so with bar highlight stopping at cap_x, those pixels reveal LcarsBlockBg (black) as square notches instead of a smooth round terminus.

## Constraints for the real fix
- Must not paint a solid highlight over the cap image at higher priority than the image.
- Must produce a rounded terminus (no black square corners).
- Must survive viewport scroll (i.e., not depend on the cap's screen position matching an extmark's buffer position — that fails under scroll anyway, and is what caused this regression to be visible).

## Possible directions (do not lock in — see AGENTS.md, no prescriptive fixes)
- Bake periwinkle into the cap PNG's outer-corner pixels so no cell needs a background behind them.
- Paint a 2-cell periwinkle extmark on the cap cells at a lower priority than the image, if image.nvim exposes a way to render images above extmarks (needs verification).
- Confirm whether the "sharp corner" 2b was ever visible on Tab A before this session, or whether it only appeared in a specific screenshot scale — the original observation may have been marginal.

## Verification for close
- Cap visible on Tab A header (block 1, rows 1-2) and footer (block 1, rows 17-18) without scrolling.
- No black square corners at the cap's outer edges.
- Regression check: scroll viewport right by 20 cols, caps still align with the elbow structure.
close_reason: Fixed via bar_w = cap_x - bar_x0 in nvim/lua/lcars/block_demo.lua make_A. Bar highlight now stops one cell short of the 2-cell vcap so both cap cells fall back to LcarsBlockBg (black), letting the vcap PNG's semicircle render intact (periwinkle interior, transparent outer corners over black). Verified pixel-precise on all 6 caps (3 blocks × header+footer) at narrow (bw=32) and full window widths. Sign-off received.

title: LCARS input-panel theming for nvim command buffer (winhighlight orange stem)
description: Add winhighlight overrides in command_buffer.lua so the command buffer reads as an LCARS input panel: orange left stem (LcarsCmdStem replaces periwinkle LineNr/SignColumn), dark amber cursor line (LcarsCmdCursorLine), signcolumn pinned to yes:1 so the stem never collapses. No changes to lcars.conf or normal nvim sessions — all overrides are window-local via winhighlight.

title: LCARS theming for the command buffer split and surrounding chrome
description: The nvim command buffer panel and its surrounding kitty split should look like part of the LCARS interface — consistent with the existing prompt theming. This may involve changes to the existing zsh prompt, the kitty tab/border styling, or nvim statusline. Goal is visual coherence: the command area reads as an LCARS panel, not a bare terminal.
notes: Added laststatus=0 to nvim launch -c flags in kitty/lcarcat.keybindings.conf. Both tabline and statusline are now suppressed in the command buffer split. Deployed and ready to validate.

title: Auto-resize nvim command panel as content grows beyond minimum lines
description: When the nvim buffer content exceeds a minimum line threshold (e.g. 2 lines), dynamically expand the bottom panel and shrink the panels above it. Shrink back when content decreases. Use kitty's resize-window action or a hook in nvim's TextChanged event to trigger the resize.

title: Keybinding to submit nvim buffer content as shell command
description: Implement the submit flow: a keybinding (e.g. <leader>Enter or a kitty shortcut) reads the nvim buffer content, sends it to a designated shell panel via kitty's send-text or kitten, and optionally clears the buffer. Must handle multi-line commands correctly.
design: Submit keybinding sends buffer content to the kitty pane directly above the command buffer. Default behavior: keep the submitted command in the buffer (do not clear). A separate 'send and clear' variant may be added later. Multi-line commands must be handled correctly. The existing lcarcat-z2g bead covers appending to a history file.

title: Pin nvim command buffer panel to bottom of kitty layout
description: Create a persistent kitty panel (horizontal split at bottom) that runs an nvim instance configured as a command input buffer. The panel should appear on a keybinding, stay pinned, and not interfere with the primary work panels above it. Configure nvim to start in insert mode with a single scratch buffer for command input.
design: Mode is opt-in: user launches the command buffer mode explicitly (keybinding TBD). On entry, the kitty window gets a horizontal split at the bottom running an nvim instance; the existing shell scrollback stays above. Panel is persistent for the duration of the mode session. In a single-window layout, one nvim buffer appears below the shell. In a two-split side-by-side layout, each split gets its own nvim command buffer below it. The nvim instance loads the full user config (some features may be hidden/disabled later). Mode exit is deferred to a future bead.
notes: Implemented as ctrl+a>b in kitty/lcarcat.keybindings.conf. Uses launch --location=hsplit --bias=20 (4-line starting height). Nvim launched with buftype=nofile bufhidden=hide noswapfile and startinsert. File is now deployed via deploy.sh and included from kitty.conf.
close_reason: Implemented ctrl+a>b in kitty/lcarcat.keybindings.conf (launch --location=hsplit --bias=6, nvim scratch buffer in insert mode). File added to deploy.sh mappings and included from kitty.conf. Validated live — panel opens at ~4 rows.

title: Buffer-below-shell: lightweight nvim command panel
description: Replace the readline/zsh vi-mode command input with a dedicated nvim instance pinned to the bottom of the kitty layout. The nvim buffer provides full syntax highlighting, linting, and editing capabilities. A keybinding submits the buffer content as a command to a shell panel. The panel auto-resizes as content grows, and integrates with zsh history for incremental search.

title: Cross-language single source of truth: palette, asset naming, shared constants
description:
Flag 2, cross-language half. Four separate things are duplicated across Lua, zsh, Python
and kitty conf, all enforced by hand and by comment.

1. ASSET FILENAME FORMAT — three independent encoders of one structured format:
     generate/gen_swoops.py:93   asset_name()          the generator, source of truth
     nvim/lua/lcars/assets.lua:49 M.asset_name()       hand-maintained Lua mirror
     zsh/prompt_lcars.zsh:37-40                        inline string interpolation,
                                                       not even a function
   gen_swoops.py:110 says "keep this format and the Lua mirror in chrome/assets in sync"
   — and does not mention the zsh consumer at all.

   This is the highest-severity item: a colour mismatch gives a wrong shade, but an
   asset-name mismatch gives a MISSING PNG — silent fallback or broken render.

2. GEOMETRY CONSTANTS crossing the language boundary:
     zsh _LCARS_ELBOW=5 / _LCARS_CAP=2   ==   Lua ELBOW_W=5 / CAP_W=2

3. PALETTE — palette.lua <-> prompt_lcars.zsh:25-34 <-> kitty/lcars.conf:12-37 <->
   colors/lcars.lua (16-colour block). palette.lua:5 states it outright: "Kept in sync
   with those by hand; there is no cross-language import." colors/lcars.lua:19 repeats it
   for the kitty 16-colour set.

4. CELL DIMENSIONS — 19x38 baked into asset filenames, probed independently by zsh
   (CSI 16t, see the csi-16t-cell-size-probe memory) and by Lua (image.nvim
   term.get_size). Related: lcarcat-ul0 (font-geometry epic).

DIRECTION (not decided — needs a call)
Generate the zsh and Lua constant/format files from one source rather than maintaining
mirrors. gen_swoops.py already owns the canonical asset_name(), so it is the natural
generator. Open: whether generated files are committed (simple, no build step at install)
or generated at deploy time (deploy.sh already exists and runs on every change).

Scope this deliberately — it is the piece with the most machinery and the least urgency.
Item 1 alone may be worth doing on its own.

Related: lcarcat-qm0.10 (the within-Lua half), lcarcat-6yz (packaging), lcarcat-ul0.

title: Split prompt_lcars.zsh: headless data/OSC layer shared with the image prompt
description:
>>> SETH HAS A SPECIFIC DIRECTION HERE AND MORE THOUGHTS TO EXPLAIN. Ask him
>>> before designing past this description. The shape below is his steer, not a
>>> proposal to be elaborated independently.

SETH'S DIRECTION (2026-08-27)
Strip the OSC hook out into a separate, headless prompt config — data only, no
rendering, aimed at nvim — and have the full zsh image prompt SHARE that same layer
rather than duplicate it. One source of truth for prompt *data*; kitty graphics
rendering becomes a consumer sitting on top of it, not the thing the data is
entangled with.

WHY (analysis backing the direction)

prompt_lcars.zsh has become a dual-target renderer with a third job bolted on.
_lcars_swoop_precmd branches on _lcars_graphics_ok and either paints kitty graphics
(swoop bar, chip drop-priority, fill arithmetic, placeholder cells) or takes a plain
text fallback — and now, on BOTH paths, also serialises a data feed for a different
consumer entirely.

The dangerous property: the data job has no visual feedback in the environment where
the rendering job runs. If the OSC 7447 payload breaks while you are in kitty, the bar
still looks perfect and nothing tells you. You find out next time you open :LcarsTerm.

Splitting data from rendering fixes that structurally — the headless layer becomes
independently testable (feed it a state, assert on the emitted bytes) without a
terminal, kitty, or screenshots.

RELATED PROBLEMS IN THE SAME AREA (may or may not belong in this bead — ask)

- No version handshake across the boundary. Three protocols cross it: OSC 133
  (standard, borrowed), OSC 7 (standard, borrowed), OSC 7447 (ours, docs/osc-7447.md).
  nvim cannot ask "what do you speak?"; the shell cannot ask "is anyone listening?".

- deploy.sh copies the zsh half to ~/.config/zsh/ and the nvim half to ~/.config/nvim/
  with nothing checking they are the same generation. Not hypothetical: a stale
  ~/.config/nvim/lua/lcars/pty_session.lua silently hijacked the unit suite during the
  ba0 session, because -u NONE leaves that dir on runtimepath (fixed in 125e250). The
  same skew in a live session is quieter — an old nvim just shows no chips, which is
  indistinguishable from a shell that never emitted any.

- The spec's forward-compat rules (unknown kind renders with a default, unknown message
  type ignored, extra fields ignored) cover additive skew only. A grammar change has no
  path.

OPEN QUESTION THIS DECIDES
Is the shell the source of truth for prompt state with nvim as one of several consumers
— in which case the boundary deserves a real contract — or is the shell feed a bridge
until nvim computes this itself? Seth's direction implies the former. Confirm before
investing in protocol machinery.

Refs: docs/osc-7447.md, zsh/prompt_lcars.zsh (_lcars_swoop_precmd, _lcars_emit_chips,
_lcars_graphics_ok), nvim/lua/lcars/pty_session.lua

title: chrome phase 5: general pane-edge split model (VISUAL REVIEW REQUIRED)
description:
>>> SETH WANTS TO VISUALLY REVIEW THE PROPOSED CHANGES BEFORE THEY LAND. <<<
>>> He expects to agree, but wants to see mockups/screenshots first. Do NOT
>>> ship this phase on the strength of the description alone — build the
>>> mockup, show it, get the nod, then implement.

This is the only phase that changes what the screen looks like.

CURRENT MODEL — "outer frame only" (chrome.lua:156): one top-left corner, one bottom-left
corner, interior edges get capped channels. It degrades past a single split:

- frame_panes only runs for a.row == top_row and for the bottom row, so A PANE IN THE
  MIDDLE OF A 3-WAY VERTICAL STACK GETS NO CORNER TREATMENT AT ALL.
- The horizontal-separator loop breaks after the first matching window below (line 221),
  emitting one separator segment per upper window regardless of how many panes sit beneath.
- lx = (c0 == 0) and rail_width or c0 special-cases the screen's left edge, so interior and
  edge separators follow different rules.
- far_right_cap applies only to the last window in a row, leaving a middle column's right
  edge uncapped.

DESIGN-LANGUAGE INCONSISTENCY: kitty and nvim disagree about what a split looks like.
kitty (_LCARS_SPLIT_SWOOP / _lcars_detect_pane in prompt_lcars.zsh) is per-pane — an elbow
on every side that abuts another pane. nvim is one global outer frame. Same concept, two
philosophies, so a kitty split and an nvim split do not look like the same system.

PROPOSAL: adopt kitty's rule in nvim, because it is the one that generalises. Model the
screen as a set of PANE EDGES and give every edge a terminator determined only by what it
abuts:

  screen edge        -> elbow into the rail
  neighbouring pane  -> capped channel + 1-col gap
  tabline/statusline -> elbow into that bar

No special cases for "top row" or "left edge", no global outer-frame concept. A 2x2 grid
then works for the same reason a single split does, and nvim matches kitty.

Depends on phase 4: the pure plan.lua is what makes it possible to assert the edge grammar
across many topologies without screenshotting each one.

title: chrome phase 4: split compute_placements into topology -> plan -> assets
description:
compute_placements() (chrome.lua:138-310) is ~170 lines mixing five concerns: window
discovery, policy (tabline_visible, the terminal-buffer suppression), topology reasoning,
asset filename construction, and coordinate math. It reads vim state throughout, so it can
only be tested by launching a real nvim and taking a picture.

  chrome/topology.lua   vim windows -> pure layout model { panes, edges, corners }
  chrome/plan.lua       layout model + policy -> placements   (PURE, testable)
  chrome/assets.lua     placement -> asset name/path (mostly exists in assets.lua)
  chrome.lua            lifecycle, policy flags, registry registration

The win is plan.lua as a pure function: feed it a synthetic 2x2 grid, a 3-way vertical
stack, nested splits, and assert on the placement list. That is the ONLY practical way to
attack the multi-split problem in phase 5 — screenshotting every split topology does not
scale, and screenshots are exactly what let the current breakage go unnoticed.

Prerequisite for phase 5. Pure refactor, no visual change.

title: chrome phase 2: registry owns invalidation via layer dirty-specs
description:
The separator bug was a missing WinScrolled subscription. Adding the event (7701abc) is a
patch — the next component that places an image will make the same mistake, because the
rule currently exists only as a paragraph in docs/nvim-chrome.md.

Structural version: layers declare when they go dirty, and the registry runs ONE debounced
reconcile pass for all of them.

  registry.register_layer("chrome", {
    events   = { "VimResized", "WinResized", "WinNew", "WinClosed",
                 "TabEnter", "BufWinEnter", "WinEnter" },
    volatile = true,
    plan     = chrome.compute_placements,
  })

`volatile = true` is the point: "re-place me whenever ANY layer reconciles". That is exactly
the prose rule — a component placing kitty images must re-place on events that cause a
NEIGHBOUR to redraw, not only on events that change its own geometry. chrome sets it because
its images sit on rows the frame layer scrolls through; the frame layer does not need it.

Turns "remember to subscribe to your neighbour's events" from tribal knowledge into a
declaration. Keep the existing 80ms debounce semantics (chrome.lua:395-404).

title: chrome phase 1: registry becomes the only caller of image.nvim
description:
Make image_registry.lua actually be what its header already claims to be.

Blocker to fix first: registry.place() hardcodes `window = win, buffer = buf` plus a
render_offset_top = -1 workaround. chrome needs WINDOWLESS absolute-screen placement (see
chrome.lua's "+1 float trap" note) and cannot use it as written.

1. Two placement addresses, exactly one per placement:
     { win = w, buf = b, row = r, col = c }   buffer-bound, scrolls with content
     { screen_x = x, screen_y = y }           windowless, absolute cell

2. Declarative reconcile instead of imperative place/clear:
     registry.reconcile(layer, placements)
   `layer` is an owner tag ("chrome", "frame", "eob"). `placements` is the COMPLETE desired
   set for that layer; the registry diffs against the previous plan, clears what is gone,
   creates what is new, leaves unchanged handles alone. This is chrome.lua's render_all
   (329-358) generalised, so every layer gets the dedupe-by-key behaviour only chrome has.

Deletes: chrome.state.imgs, chrome.placement_key, chrome.clear_all, chrome.render_all.
Then (can be a follow-up) block_demo.tab_imgs and terminal_frame's inline table.

Pure refactor — no visual change. Verify with test/integration/terminal_win.sh plus the
separator pixel-diff check from the ba0 session.

title: (EPIC) chrome.lua image handling: one owner, testable plan, general split model
description:
chrome.lua predates the shared image/render library work and never joined it. Three
problems, in increasing order of how much design judgement they need.

1. FOUR image owners, not one. image_registry.lua's own header claims "frame_renderer,
   terminal_frame, and chrome all share a single ownership model" — that is aspirational.
   Only frame_renderer and terminal_win use it. chrome.lua:349, block_demo.lua:109 and
   terminal_frame.lua:65 each call image.from_file directly against private handle tables.
   chrome *cannot* adopt the registry as written: registry.place() hardcodes
   window/buffer binding, while chrome needs windowless absolute-screen placement.

2. The plan is untestable. compute_placements() (chrome.lua:138-310) is ~170 lines mixing
   window discovery, policy, topology reasoning, asset naming and coordinate math, reading
   vim state throughout. It can only be exercised by launching nvim and taking a picture,
   which is why multi-split breakage went unnoticed.

3. The split model is "outer frame only" and does not generalise past one split. Separately,
   nvim ("one outer frame") and kitty ("elbow on every side that abuts a pane",
   _LCARS_SPLIT_SWOOP in prompt_lcars.zsh) use different design languages for the same idea.

Motivating incident: the display/input separator losing its ends on scroll (fixed in
7701abc by adding WinScrolled to chrome's autocmd list). That was not a logic error — it
was two components writing the same screen row with no arbitration, invisible to every
state-dump assertion, surviving redraw!, and self-healing on WinEnter so it read as
flakiness. The fix was a patch; phases 1-3 are the structural version.

Phases 1-2 are pure refactor, no visual change. Phase 3 is small once 1 lands. Phase 4
unblocks 5. Phase 5 is the only one that changes what you see.

title: Regression test: chrome images cleared by a neighbour's scroll
description:
The separator-row bug (chrome elbow/cap images on the display/input separator going black after scrolling, fixed by adding WinScrolled to chrome.lua's autocmd list) is invisible to every existing assertion — it lives entirely in the kitty image layer, survives redraw!, and self-heals on WinEnter, so it cannot be caught by frame_buffer state dumps.

A working repro exists (developed in the lcarcat-ba0 session): open :LcarsTerm, run several commands to make the display scrollable, wincmd k, C-u x4, screenshot, then measure the separator row.

The assertion that worked: derive the separator's screen row from nvim window geometry (win_screenpos + height) rather than eyeballing, then pixel-diff that row's band against the pre-scroll capture. Identical = pass. Before the fix it was 10874/131328 px different; after, 0.

Turn that into test/integration/chrome_scroll_separator.sh. The geometry-derived-row + pixel-diff-against-baseline technique generalizes to any 'image layer got clobbered' bug and is worth having as a reusable helper.

title: term_input: set filetype to zsh/bash to match the running shell
description:
term_input.lua's input buffer has no filetype set. terminal_win.lua spawns the PTY with vim.env.SHELL or '/bin/zsh' (terminal_win.lua ~line 193), so the input buffer's content is shell syntax matching whatever that resolves to -- but there's no syntax highlighting for it since filetype is unset.

Set the input buffer's filetype from the same shell_cmd used to start the PTY: derive the basename (zsh/bash/etc), map to the matching nvim filetype ('zsh' or 'bash'; fall back to 'sh' for anything else), and set it via vim.bo[buf].filetype in term_input.lua's M.open() (or have terminal_win.lua pass it through opts, matching how it already passes win/on_submit/min_height/max_height).
acceptance_criteria: Typing a shell command in the term_input buffer shows shell syntax highlighting (strings, comments, $VARS) matching the actual shell (zsh vs bash), not plain text.
notes: Implemented: terminal_win.lua now derives shell_cmd once (vim.env.SHELL or /bin/zsh), computes its basename, and passes filetype='zsh'|'bash'|'sh' through term_input.open()'s opts (mirroring how win/on_submit/min_height/max_height are already threaded). term_input.lua sets vim.bo[buf].filetype = opts.filetype when provided -- optional, so existing callers/tests that don't pass it are unaffected. Both files syntax-checked clean via nvim --headless loadfile().
close_reason: Fixed: terminal_win.lua derives filetype (zsh/bash/sh) from the shell_cmd used to start the PTY and passes it through to term_input.open(). User confirmed syntax highlighting works in a live session.

title: terminal-win: PTY width should be the frame's content width, not the raw window width
description:
Found while manually testing :LcarsTerm (lcarcat-2z9): `ls` output runs off
the right edge of the window.

Root cause: terminal_win.lua's M.open() sizes the PTY from the raw display
window width —

  local width = vim.api.nvim_win_get_width(display_win)
  pty_session.start(shell, { width = width, height = height }, callbacks)

— but that's not the width actually visible inside the frame. Two things
eat into it that this calculation ignores:

1. frame_buffer's own bar width (bw) is computed as
   `vim.api.nvim_win_get_width(display_win) - 14` (reserves margin for the
   header/footer's elbow+cap images) — terminal_win.lua already does this
   subtraction for bw, but never applies anything equivalent to the PTY
   width it passes to pty_session.start().
2. Content lines get an additional left indent before any real text:
   frame_renderer.render_content() writes `pad(lp) .. " " .. l` (lp=6, so
   real content starts at column 7).

Tools like `ls` query the PTY's reported width (COLUMNS / ioctl TIOCGWINSZ)
to size their multi-column output — with the current (too-wide) value, `ls`
formats assuming more horizontal room than the frame's content area
actually has, and the display window has wrap=false, so the overflow is
clipped invisibly off the right edge rather than wrapping.

Fix direction: PTY width should be based on the frame's actual content
width, roughly `window_width - lp - 1` for the left margin — verify
empirically against a real wide-output command (`ls`, `ls -la` in a big
directory) whether the right side should also stay within bw's boundary
for visual consistency with the header/footer bar, rather than assuming
the formula without checking. Height wasn't reported as an issue but is
worth a quick sanity check too, since it's computed the same
unadjusted way.
notes:
Fixed and verified empirically (2026-08-27).

GEOMETRY, in window cols (0-indexed from window-left, incl. the 1-col
statuscolumn gutter — same convention as frame_renderer):
  bar        lp .. lp+bw-1        (lp=6, bw=win_width-14)
  content    lp+2 .. lp+bw-1      (frame_buffer writes an lp+1-space prefix in
                                   BUFFER cols = window col lp+2)
  => content_width = bw - 2

terminal_win.lua now has a geometry(win) helper returning lp, bw,
content_width; pty_session.start() gets content_width instead of the raw
window width.

EMPIRICAL RESULTS at win_width=181 (bw=167, content_width=165), via the new
test/integration/terminal_win_pty_width.sh:
  - 'tput cols' inside the session reports 165 (was 181).
  - A ruler line of exactly $COLUMNS chars renders with its last char at
    terminal col 172 — the frame's right edge, where the header vcap (cols
    171-172) and footer cap (col 172) images sit. Col 173 is empty. Confirmed
    with get_cell_grid.py, not just arithmetic.
  - 'ls /usr/bin': widest output line 136 cols, well inside 165, no clipping.
    (First run measured raw rec.lines including ANSI — 221 'cols' — which is a
    measurement artifact, not overflow; the test now strips ANSI, since baleia
    strips it before the buffer sees it.)

ANSWER TO THE OPEN QUESTION IN THE DESCRIPTION: yes, the right side should stay
within bw's boundary. Content now ends flush with the bar's right edge. Note the
left inset is 2 cols (stem at lp, one space at lp+1) but that is structural, not
decorative — there is no stem on the right, so 'flush' is not asymmetric.
If a decorative right margin is wanted instead, content_width becomes bw-4.

HEIGHT: left as the raw window height. It only feeds full-screen TUI apps
(none supported yet — nothing scrolls the PTY's own screen), and the frame
chrome eating rows does not clip anything today. Follow-up noted on qm0.5.
close_reason: PTY width now sized from the frame's content width (bw-2); verified empirically at win_width=181 (tput cols=165, full-width line lands flush on the frame's right edge at terminal col 172, ls /usr/bin no clipping). New regression test test/integration/terminal_win_pty_width.sh.

title: terminal frame images don't scroll/hide with the display buffer
description:
image_registry.place() uses image.nvim's absolute x/y floating placement,
not scroll-following Unicode placeholders — contradicts the design doc's
"Why Unicode placeholder images, not absolute placement" section. Images
are positioned once at placement time using the window's topline; never
repositioned afterward.

Discovered while manually testing :LcarsTerm (lcarcat-2z9).

Symptoms:
- Switching buffers in the display window leaves old elbow/cap images
  floating over whatever buffer is now shown there.
- Manually scrolling the display window (e.g. zt) leaves images pinned
  at their original screen row while the text scrolls underneath them.
- Compounds with terminal_win.lua's scroll-to-bottom-on-output behavior
  (added in 2z9): more frequent scrolling makes the detached-image
  artifact show up more often, not less.

Fix direction: chrome.lua already solves this exact problem for its own
images via clear_all()+render_all() wired to WinScrolled/BufWinEnter/
WinEnter/WinResized/etc (see chrome.lua:428-441). Add a
frame_buffer.reposition_images() that iterates M.blocks and re-places
each block's images at the current window scroll offset (clearing stale
image keys first via renderer.clear_images), then wire terminal_win.lua's
display window to the same autocmd set, calling reposition_images() and
clearing images on BufLeave/WinLeave from the display buffer.
notes:
Follow-up from user's manual test (fresh nvim instance):

1. VERTICAL OFFSET (fixed): header/footer bg bars were 1 row higher than the elbow/cap images. Root-caused to an off-by-one in the installed image.nvim (3rd/image.nvim @ 5c6f29a, 2026-08-19): renderer.lua's window+buffer-bound 'on topline' branch (~line 266, absolute_y = win_info.winrow) and its normal fully-visible branch (~line 344, absolute_y = screen_pos.row) both assign a 1-indexed getwininfo/screenpos row straight into absolute_y without the -1 the kitty backend expects (backends/kitty/init.lua:154 does write_graphics_at(cfg, x+1, y+1), confirming 0-indexed input). image.nvim's own partial-scroll branch (line 324) already has an explicit -1 and wasn't affected. Worked around in nvim/lua/lcars/image_registry.lua by passing render_offset_top = -1 to image.from_file() -- that option is added to absolute_y in exactly the two buggy branches and explicitly skipped during real partial-scroll clipping (renderer.lua:348), so it's a scoped correction, not a blind offset. Did not touch input y (buf_row) directly since that also feeds topline/botline branch-selection comparisons and would have desynced those instead.

2. HORIZONTAL SCROLL (mitigated, not fixed): user confirmed images don't track horizontal scroll and okayed just disabling it for now (separate bead already covers output-width handling for the actual long-line root cause). Added a WinScrolled autocmd in terminal_win.lua's M.open() scoped to display_win that snaps leftcol back to 0 via winrestview whenever it drifts -- self-limiting (no leftcol change -> no further event). Vertical scrolling untouched.

Changed further: nvim/lua/lcars/image_registry.lua (render_offset_top=-1 in M.place's image.from_file() opts), nvim/lua/lcars/terminal_win.lua (WinScrolled leftcol-pin autocmd in M.open()).

Still needs the human capture-test pass from the first note (frame_renderer.sh/frame_buffer.sh + scroll-back-to-top + buffer-switch) -- please re-check vertical alignment specifically now that render_offset_top is in place, and confirm horizontal scroll no longer drags images. Still IN_PROGRESS, not committed.
close_reason: Fixed: switched to image.nvim window+buffer-bound placement, corrected upstream off-by-one via render_offset_top=-1, pinned horizontal scroll. User confirmed visually in a fresh nvim instance.

title: term-input: theme gutter-EOB-fill backfill + elbow/header/footer chrome
description:
term_input.lua's orange styling is incomplete, and it has no framing chrome
at all. Feedback from Seth after reviewing the merged lyz implementation:

1. The input panel's "stem" has TWO areas that both need to be orange:
   - The built-in gutter (LineNr/SignColumn cells, where ruler lines
     appear) — this IS orange already, via term_input.open()'s winhighlight
     (LineNr/SignColumn -> LcarsTermInputStem).
   - The gutter-EOB-fill backfill (nvim/lua/lcars/gutter_eob_fill.lua) —
     fills the area between the end of the gutter and the end of the
     window on below-end-of-buffer rows, via a style="minimal" floating
     window. This is currently periwinkle, not orange, because its float
     hardcodes winhighlight = "Normal:SignColumn,NormalNC:SignColumn,
     EndOfBuffer:SignColumn" — it resolves the GLOBAL "SignColumn"
     highlight group by name, not through whatever window-local
     winhighlight remapping the window it's filling for has set up. It has
     no concept of a per-window override today.

2. Overall framing: the elbow images, header bar, and footer bar around
   the input panel should be periwinkle (the standard LCARS frame color —
   matching frame_buffer's display window chrome) — orange is reserved for
   the stem alone, to mark "this is the input panel." term_input.lua
   currently has zero framing chrome (no elbows, no header/footer bars) —
   it's a bare highlighted split.

## Likely approach (needs design review before implementing)

- gutter_eob_fill.lua needs some notion of a per-window highlight-group
  override (e.g. a registration table window id -> override group name)
  so its float can resolve to LcarsTermInputStem instead of the global
  SignColumn, OR term_input.lua manages its own EOB fill independently of
  the generic global mechanism. Trade-off between a shared mechanism vs.
  input-panel-specific code needs a decision.
- Header/footer/elbow chrome: reuse the pattern in
  nvim/lua/lcars/frame_renderer.lua (render_header, render_footer,
  place_images, elbow_path/felbow_path) and image_registry.lua's PNG
  transmit/cache, adapted for a much shorter panel (term_input is a
  handful of rows, not a scrolling block history).

## Do not implement without design sign-off

Seth wants to review design changes to the input panel's top and bottom
bars before implementation — this is explicitly NOT a "figure it out and
build it" task. Raise the design questions (chrome layout for a short
fixed-height panel, whether/how it echoes frame_buffer's header/footer
shape) before writing code.

title: terminal-frame: resize detection + image invalidation on VimResized
description:
Wire up font/window resize detection in terminal_frame.lua so that image
assets are invalidated and regenerated when cell pixel dimensions change.

On VimResized autocmd (already registered in M.setup()):
  1. Re-probe cell dims via assets.cell_px() (CSI 16t query)
  2. Compare against image_registry's stored current_cw/current_ch
  3. If changed: call image_registry.M.reset(), then M.refresh()
     — refresh() will call get_id() which generates missing assets on cache miss

This makes font zoom (ctrl+shift+= / ctrl+shift+-) and display changes
seamless: the next refresh picks up the new dims, regenerates PNGs if needed,
and retransmits at the correct pixel size.

Failure handling: CSI 16t probe can time out on non-kitty terminals — keep
the existing dims and skip invalidation rather than clearing a working cache.

Depends on lcarcat-qm0.4 (generate-on-miss) — resize detection is only useful
once get_id() can generate missing assets.
notes:
Also resize the PTY on VimResized, not just images:
terminal_win.lua's geometry(win) helper returns (lp, bw, content_width);
pty_session needs a resize path (vim.fn.jobresize) fed with content_width and
the new window height. Without it the PTY keeps the width it was started with
and COLUMNS-aware tools mis-format after a resize (context: lcarcat-wve).

title: image-registry: generate missing PNGs on cache miss
description:
Extend image_registry.lua (lcarcat-ry7) so that get_id() generates missing
PNG assets before transmitting, instead of silently failing.

When get_id(asset_name, cw, ch) is called and the expected PNG file does not
exist on disk, invoke gen_swoops.py synchronously via vim.fn.system() before
proceeding with the APC transmit.

Generator invocation mirrors zsh/prompt_lcars.zsh's _lcars_ensure_assets():
  vim.fn.system({
    'uv', 'run', '--with', 'pillow', gen_py,
    '--color', color, '--outdir', cache_dir,
    '--cellw', cw, '--cellh', ch
  })

Fail gracefully: if uv or gen_swoops.py is missing, log a warning and return
nil from get_id() — callers must already handle nil (no image to place).

Depends on lcarcat-ry7 (image-registry base implementation).

title: Per-row image placement for progressive viewport clipping
description:
image.nvim hides an image entirely when its buffer anchor row scrolls above the viewport topline — there is no partial clipping. For LCARS elbow/hcap chrome, this means the full 3-row elbow disappears as soon as row 0 scrolls off, rather than showing rows 1-2 while row 0 is hidden.

Fix: place one image.nvim from_file() per elbow row instead of one image for the full elbow. A 3-row elbow becomes three 5x1 placements, each anchored to its own buffer row (y=0, y=1, y=2). As the buffer scrolls, row 0 disappears first, then row 1, then row 2 — clean progressive clipping with no custom math.

image_registry.lua should expose a place_image(buf, win, path, row, col, w) call that issues one placement per source row. frame_renderer.lua calls it once per elbow/hcap row when building the header/footer.

Acceptance:
- Elbow PNG placed as 3 separate 5x1 images anchored to buffer rows 0/1/2
- Scrolling up past the header clips row by row (row 0 hides first, rows 1+2 remain)
- No custom WinScrolled autocmd needed — image.nvim handles re-render

Informed by spike-1 findings (lcarcat-zi1).

title: LCARS nvim terminal frame
description:
Build a live nvim-native LCARS-framed terminal — a replacement for the standard :terminal that renders each shell command's output inside LCARS chrome (elbow PNG header, periwinkle bar, chip pills, stem column, hcap footer), with a sticky orange-stem input buffer at the bottom.

## Architecture

- Custom nvim buffer (not :terminal) + jobstart(pty=true)
- OSC 133 A/B/C/D marks parsed from raw PTY bytes → block lifecycle events
- baleia.nvim for ANSI SGR → extmarks
- Unicode placeholder protocol for elbow/hcap PNGs (scroll with content)
- Separate term_input.lua for the input panel (command_buffer.lua untouched)

## Block states

| state   | header/stem color |
|---------|-------------------|
| live    | sage              |
| done    | periwinkle        |
| failed  | red               |

## Files (all new except deploy.sh + lcars.lua)

  block_record.lua     — A→D data model
  image_registry.lua   — PNG transmit + kitty image ID cache
  frame_renderer.lua   — pure render: header/content/footer into buffer
  frame_buffer.lua     — display buffer owner; append/update blocks
  pty_session.lua      — PTY job + OSC 133 parser + carry-buffer
  term_input.lua       — orange-stem input panel, chansend submit
  terminal_win.lua     — layout + wiring; :LcarsTerm command

block_demo.lua removed from deploy.sh (kept in repo for reference).

## Minimal demo acceptance

  1. :LcarsTerm → ls → header on command start, stem on output, footer on exit
  2. false → red header/footer
  3. ping 8.8.8.8 → sage live block, ▌ cursor, no footer; ^C → closes
  4. Scroll: elbow PNGs scroll with content, not floating

## Backlog (deferred, separate child beads)

  stderr-separation, fold-unfold, block-navigation, alternate-screen passthrough,
  multi-session, cmd-in-header, live-update debounce,
  spike-3 (nvim_open_term transclude escape hatch)

## Key research (docs/nvim-terminal-research.md)

  - nvim terminal.txt lines 203-247: OSC 133 + TermRequest
  - channel.txt lines 1-140: PTY stderr merge caveat
  - api.txt line 1260: nvim_open_term (escape hatch path)
  - baleia.nvim: buf_set_lines() / buf_set_text() wrappers
  - molten-nvim: reference for block-framed output with image.nvim

title: terminal-win: layout manager wiring all pieces into :LcarsTerm
description:
Create nvim/lua/lcars/terminal_win.lua

Depends on: frame-buffer (lcarcat-tq2), pty-session (lcarcat-unk), term-input (lcarcat-lyz).

M.open():
  1. Create frame_buffer, open display buffer in top split (modifiable=false, periwinkle SignColumn)
  2. Start pty_session with $SHELL
  3. Register callbacks: on_prompt_start/on_command_start/on_output_line/on_command_done → frame_buffer methods
  4. Open term_input split below

User command: :LcarsTerm

Acceptance (integration milestone):
  1. :LcarsTerm → type ls → header appears on command start, output lines with stem, footer closes on exit
  2. Type false → header and footer render in red
  3. Type ping 8.8.8.8 → sage live block, cursor ▌, no footer; ^C → block closes
  4. Scroll up through multiple completed blocks — elbow PNGs scroll with content, not floating
notes:
lcarcat-lyz resolved its API to a callback contract: term_input.open(buf, opts)
where opts = { win, on_submit, min_height, max_height }. term_input.lua does
NOT require pty_session or terminal_win by name, and never touches
block_record.

When implementing terminal_win.lua, pass on_submit as a wrapper, not
term_input reaching out to you:

  term_input.open(buf, {
    win = input_win,
    on_submit = function(cmd_text)
      rec.command = cmd_text
      pty_session.send(cmd_text)
    end,
  })

This is how rec.command gets set on the live block_record before the PTY
executes the command. See lyz's --design field for the full resolved
contract (highlight group names, resize/clamp behavior, post-submit clear).
When writing capture/integration tests for terminal_win.lua, read docs/testing.md's "Known gotchas for scripted nvim/PTY tests" section first (also bd memory key nvim-pty-test-gotchas) — covers startinsert/Ex-command collisions, background-job window-focus lookup, screenshot capture from a background job, and pty_session cold-start timing. All discovered building lyz's integration test.
Pre-flight for implementation (gaps in the pseudocode/docs worth knowing up front):

1. frame_buffer.new(opts) needs `bw` (bar width) sized explicitly for a real
   window — its default (60) is far narrower than a real nvim window
   (pty_session defaults width=220). Compute it like
   frame_buffer_test.lua does: bw = vim.api.nvim_win_get_width(display_win) - 14.

comments.author: Seth Woodworth
comments.text:
Implemented terminal_win.lua per the wiring-notes contract, plus the three
resolved scope calls: :LcarsTerm reuses an existing session instead of
opening a second one; pty_session.start() is sized from the real display
window's width/height (resize-on-VimResized stays deferred to qm0.5);
closing either window (WinClosed autocmd) stops the PTY and closes the
sibling window.

While verifying against a real shell, found and fixed three pre-existing
bugs blocking end-to-end verification (all upstream of this bead's own
file, in the already-closed lcarcat-unk):

1. pty_session.lua's on_stdout never flushed a line. nvim's on_stdout
   already splits the raw byte stream on "\n" before the callback sees
   `data`, but _parse_chunk expects to find literal \n bytes itself to
   detect line boundaries. Fixed by rejoining `data` with "\n"
   (table.concat) before parsing.
2. OSC 133 marks never reached the nested shell at all. Kitty's
   shell-integration only auto-injects into a shell it directly spawns as
   a pane's child; a shell spawned by pty_session.start() is a nested
   child of nvim's own job and never gets it. Fixed by adding
   precmd/preexec/OSC-7 hooks directly to zsh/prompt_lcars.zsh, ordered so
   the prompt's own chrome (swoop bar, STARDATE line) is dropped rather
   than leaking into captured command output (relies on the same
   skip_lines window pty_session already uses for echoed input, plus the
   fact that no block is open between D and A).
3. A trailing \r held in carry across a chunk boundary could leak into
   emitted line text as a literal ^M when the flush was triggered by a
   bare \n or an OSC start rather than the paired \r\n case. Fixed with a
   strip_trailing_cr() helper at both flush sites.

Added 2 regression unit tests (test/unit/pty_parser_test.lua, 32/32
passing) and a new integration test (test/integration/terminal_win.sh)
that verifies end-to-end against a real shell — open, ls success (done/
periwinkle), false failure (failed/red), session reuse, cleanup-on-close,
reopen-after-cleanup — no stubs.

After manual live testing turned up further issues:
- ls output colors were unreadable (baleia falls back to a generic
  default ANSI theme since vim.g.terminal_color_N was never set). Fixed:
  nvim/colors/lcars.lua now sets terminal_color_0..15 to match
  kitty/lcars.conf's palette.
- Display window never auto-scrolled to follow new output. Fixed:
  terminal_win.lua now moves the display window's cursor to the last
  line after every append/open/close-block event; locked in with a new
  cursor_at_end assertion in the integration test.
- Kitty images (elbow/cap) don't scroll or get cleared when switching
  buffers or scrolling the display window — image_registry.place() uses
  image.nvim's absolute x/y floating placement, not the scroll-following
  Unicode placeholder approach docs/nvim-terminal-frame.md says this
  system should use. Bigger than a wiring fix (needs a new
  frame_buffer.reposition_images() API + autocmd wiring, following
  chrome.lua's existing pattern) — filed as lcarcat-382 rather than fixed
  here.
- Chips are unimplemented (rec.chips renders when populated but nothing
  populates it) and Seth flagged the live-block append rendering style as
  something he wants to revisit — filed as a placeholder,
  lcarcat-ba0, pending his feedback before any design/implementation.

and 4 (scroll through multiple blocks) were only checked visually via

title: term-input: orange-stem input panel submitting to PTY
description:
Create nvim/lua/lcars/term_input.lua

New file — does NOT touch command_buffer.lua (preserved for kitty send-text workflow).

Orange-stem input panel (same visual as command_buffer.lua but submits to PTY).

API:
  M.open(pty_session) → creates fixed-height split below display, applies winhighlight
  M.submit() → calls pty_session.send(buf_contents)

Reuse patterns from command_buffer.lua:
  - winhighlight for LcarsCmdStem / LcarsCmdStemDim
  - signcolumn=yes:1
  - Telescope history search
  - resize() debounce on TextChanged

Key difference from command_buffer.lua: submit() uses pty_session.send() not kitty @ send-text.
design:
RESOLVED API (supersedes original description and the 2026-08-25 comment):

M.open(buf, opts) — opts = { win, on_submit, min_height = 4, max_height = 10 }
  - buf/win are created by the caller (terminal_win.lua, or a test harness
    standing in for it) — term_input.lua does NOT call nvim_open_win itself.
  - opts.on_submit(cmd_text) is a plain callback. term_input never requires
    pty_session or terminal_win by name.
  - In the real system, terminal_win.lua passes a wrapper as on_submit that
    sets rec.command = cmd_text THEN calls pty_session.send(cmd_text) — this
    is how rec.command gets set before the PTY executes (the concern the
    2026-08-25 comment raised). block_record is owned entirely by
    terminal_win.lua; term_input.lua never references it.
  - Before terminal_win.lua (lcarcat-2z9) exists, a test script can stand in
    for it: create the split/buffer itself, pass
    on_submit = pty_session.send directly. Proves the input->PTY path works
    end-to-end (real shell execution) with no framed display yet.

M.submit() — reads buf, strips trailing blanks, joins lines with \n, calls
  opts.on_submit(text), then CLEARS the buffer to a single blank line
  (fresh-prompt UX — differs from command_buffer.lua, which leaves submitted
  text in place).

Keymap convention same as command_buffer.lua: multi-line buffer, normal-mode
<CR> submits, insert-mode <CR> inserts a newline.

New highlight groups (not LcarsCmdStem*, to avoid sharing global state with
the kitty-pane command buffer): LcarsTermInputStem, LcarsTermInputStemDim,
LcarsTermInputCursorNr, LcarsTermInputCursorLine.
notes:
Verified end-to-end via test/integration/term_input.sh (LCARCAT_SKIP_SCREENSHOTS=1):
PASS — a command typed into the input buffer and submitted via normal-mode
<CR> reaches a real PTY shell and executes (marker-file assertion).

Two bugs found and fixed during verification, both in the TEST fixture, not
in term_input.lua itself:
1. test/integration/term_input_test.lua originally called
   vim.cmd('startinsert') at the end of the :luafile execution — this
   doesn't stick (nvim reverts to Normal mode when the outer ex-command
   returns), and even deferring via vim.schedule left the buffer in
   Insert mode by the time the script's own nvim_check_messages ran its
   `:redir ... | messages` Ex command, which then got typed as literal
   text into the input buffer instead of executing. Fixed by not having
   the fixture touch insert mode at all — the driving shell script already
   sends its own explicit Esc+i before typing, which is deterministic.
2. The shared _nvim_focused_window_id helper (is_focused-based) returns
   nothing when kitty is launched from a background/non-interactive
   session — the window never receives real OS focus. term_input.sh
   resolves the window by id directly instead (there's only ever one).

Known environment limitation, not a code bug: live screenshot capture
(screencapture -l<id>) is unreliable in this background-job context —
"could not create image from window" even after Screen Recording
permission was granted, likely because an unfocused fullscreen window
isn't actually composited. test/integration/term_input.sh still captures
screenshots by default (LCARCAT_SKIP_SCREENSHOTS=1 to skip) — run it
interactively for the visual check (orange stem, buffer clears on submit).

Still pending before close: user sign-off per ticket-close-protocol.

title: pty-session: PTY job + OSC 133 parser + line carry-buffer
description:
Create nvim/lua/lcars/pty_session.lua

jobstart(shell, {pty=true}). This is the riskiest primitive — bytes arrive in chunks, not complete lines.

Responsibilities:
- Carry-buffer for incomplete escape sequences across on_stdout chunks
- Line splitter: split on \r\n, carry partial last line
- OSC 133 state machine:
    \x1b]133;A → on_prompt_start()
    \x1b]133;B → on_command_start(command_text)
    \x1b]133;C → on_command_exec()
    \x1b]133;D;N → on_command_done(exit_code)
- Everything else (non-OSC bytes) forwarded to on_output_line(line) callback
- M.send(text) → chansend(job_id, text .. '\n')

API:
  M.start(shell_cmd, callbacks) → starts PTY job
  M.send(text) → writes to PTY stdin
  M.stop() → jobstop
notes: Schema note (from b3r): block_record now includes command_start and command_end (epoch seconds) alongside duration (derived). pty_session must set rec.command_start at OSC 133;B and rec.command_end + rec.duration at OSC 133;D. duration = command_end - command_start. All three fields are nil in block_record.new().

2. A trailing \r held in carry across a chunk boundary could leak into

title: frame-buffer: display buffer owning append/update of blocks
description:
Create nvim/lua/lcars/frame_buffer.lua

Depends on frame-renderer (lcarcat-8pi).

Owns a single nvim buffer (modifiable=false except during writes).
Holds ordered list of block_records.

API:
  M.new() → creates buffer, returns frame_buffer instance
  M.open_block(rec) → writes header + 1 gap row, stores rec.buf_start
  M.append_line(rec, text) → baleia writes one content line with stem extmark
  M.close_block(rec) → re-renders header (finalize state color), writes footer, stores rec.buf_end
  M.buf → the nvim buffer number (for display in a window)

title: frame-renderer: pure render header/content/footer into buffer
description:
Create nvim/lua/lcars/frame_renderer.lua

Depends on image-registry (lcarcat-ry7) and spike-2 (lcarcat-dk5).
Reuse from block_demo.lua: chips_block() pattern, capcols() math, chip/bar highlight logic.

Pure function: given (buf, start_row, block_record) → writes lines, returns row count consumed.

render_header(buf, row, rec):
  3 lines — row 0: placeholder cells for elbow PNG + periwinkle bar fill + chip pills
  rows 1-2: per Tab A geometry from block_demo

render_content(buf, row, rec):
  one line per output entry, stem extmark at col 0

render_footer(buf, row, rec):
  1 line with hcap placeholder cells

render_live_cursor(buf, row):
  virtual text ▌ on last content line

State → color:
  live    = sage header/footer + sage stem
  done    = periwinkle header/footer + periwinkle stem
  failed  = red header/footer + red stem
notes: Schema note (from b3r): block_record now has command_start, command_end (epoch seconds), and duration (derived seconds, nil until block closes). render_header/chip pills can display duration once rec.state is done or failed — duration will be non-nil at that point.

title: image-registry: transmit elbow/hcap PNGs once per session

title: spike-1: Unicode placeholder transmission from Lua
description:
Verify that image.nvim from_file() places an elbow PNG in a scratch buffer and scrolls correctly with the buffer via WinScrolled re-render.

FINDINGS:

What works:
- image.nvim from_file() with window+buffer+x/y binding renders immediately (no scroll required)
- WinScrolled re-render is handled by image.nvim's global autocmd — no manual hook needed
- io.write(apc_escape) transmission works from Lua; asset path, cell dims, and base64 all function correctly

What doesn't work / key findings:
- Unicode placeholder via extmark/highlight: termguicolors=true forces nvim to emit \e[38;2;r;g;b;m always; kitty needs \e[38;5;<id>m — incompatible, extmarks cannot carry the image ID
- Unicode placeholder via direct io.write after redraw!: nvim post-command update_screen() repaints over the bytes; defer_fn defers past it but the image disappears on any subsequent nvim redraw
- image.nvim does NOT partially clip images at the viewport top. When the anchor row scrolls above topline, vim.fn.screenpos() returns {row=0,col=0} and the image hides entirely — no partial overlap

Decision: use image.nvim from_file() with window+buffer binding (not unicode placeholders). For progressive clipping as the elbow scrolls off, place one image per elbow row (three 5x1 images, each anchored to its own buffer row). Tracked in child bead.

Gates confirmed:
- image_registry.lua: use from_file() directly, no custom APC layer
- frame_renderer.lua: place per-row images for header/footer elbows

title: Verify context discipline: monitor context growth during Tab A resume session
description:
Meta-task attached to the Tab A resume work. The context-discipline changes from 2026-08-14 (visual-inspector subagent, grid-inspector subagent, offset/limit read discipline, docs/block_demo split) need real-world validation on an actual working session before we treat them as proven.

## Instructions for the session that picks up 2m7.10.1

Throughout the session, self-monitor for these anti-patterns and note them:

1. Any `Read` of a PNG in the main loop → should have been delegated to `visual-inspector`.
2. Any `Read` of `nvim/lua/lcars/block_demo.lua` without `offset`/`limit` → should have grepped first, then read a bounded window.
3. Any `Read` of an observation file for a tab you weren't working on → the point of the split was to avoid this.
4. Any full `test/get_cell_grid.py --dump-grid` output in main context → should have been delegated to `grid-inspector`.
5. Any re-read of a file immediately after `Edit` → the tool harness tracks state; re-read is wasted tokens.

## What to report at session close
- Rough context percentage at session start and at close (from `/context` if the user runs it).
- Any of the 5 anti-patterns above that slipped through, with a short note on why.
- Any subagent delegation that DIDN'T work well (e.g. subagent returned too much detail; parent had to re-derive).
- Suggested tweaks to AGENTS.md "Context discipline" section or the subagent instructions in `.claude/agents/`.

## What NOT to do
- Do not restructure the discipline rules mid-session on your own; note issues and let the user decide.
- Do not skip the subagents "for speed" — the discipline is the point.

Close this bead only when the session that picks up 2m7.10.1 (right cap regression) has completed a full loop (deploy, capture, inspect, fix, verify) and the user has reviewed the context-usage report.
close_reason: Context-discipline validated against the 2m7.10.1 fix session. Anti-patterns from the watchlist: no PNGs read in main loop (visual-inspector used throughout); no unbounded block_demo.lua reads (grepped first, Read with offset/limit); no cross-tab observation reads; no full get_cell_grid.py --dump-grid in main context (grid-inspector used); no post-Edit re-reads. Delegation worked well overall. Meta-finding surfaced during the session: deploy.sh is the missing step — ~/.config/nvim/lua/lcars/block_demo.lua is a copy, not a symlink, so edits do not reach the running nvim until ./deploy.sh runs. Two undeployed verify passes made the fix appear broken. Addressed by adding an Edit|Write PostToolUse auto-deploy hook that only fires for files mapped in deploy.sh (see .claude/settings.json).

title: test/overlay_grid.py: cell-boundary grid overlay for screenshot annotation

title: block_demo: DEBUG_BG diagnostic mode to expose transparent image regions
description:
Add a module-level DEBUG_BG toggle to nvim/lua/lcars/block_demo.lua.

When DEBUG_BG = true, setup_hls() sets LcarsBlockBar, LcarsBlockStem, and LcarsBlockBg highlight backgrounds to a diagnostic color (#330033 deep purple) instead of their normal colors (periwinkle / black). Normal bg is NOT changed — only the block highlight groups.

Expose as :LcarsBlockDemoDebugBg user command that toggles the flag and calls render_all().

Motivation: transparent image corners and inner fillets are visually indistinguishable from 'image not placed at all' against a black background. With purple diagnostic highlight bg, the geometry of extmark highlights relative to images is immediately visible — showing what the highlights cover vs. do not cover, without pixel-level PNG analysis.

Example diagnosis:
- Stub row fillet area is purple → LcarsBlockBg highlight extends there (correct bg, need to check image z-order)
- Bar row shows purple where a chip gap should be black → gap cells are getting LcarsBlockBar bleed
- Cap cells are purple → bar_w extends into cap region (extmark covering the image)

## Current state (partial/wrong implementation)

title: harness: composable nvim setup scripts for single screenshots and multi-state sequences
description:
Currently each scenario script duplicates the boilerplate for launching kitty, opening nvim, navigating tabs, and checking messages. We need a library of composable setup functions that scenarios can source, covering both simple single-screenshot setups and complex multi-state sequences.

Two classes of setup needed:

1. Single-screenshot helpers (sourced functions a scenario calls):
   - nvim_open: launch nvim, wait 2.5s
   - nvim_reload_module NAME: package.loaded[NAME]=nil; require(NAME), sleep 1.0
   - nvim_goto_tab N: nvim_set_current_tabpage(list[N]), sleep 1.0
   - nvim_check_messages: redir messages to /tmp, grep for errors, abort if found
   - nvim_run_cmd CMD: send :CMD\r, sleep 0.5

2. Multi-state sequence helpers (for testing state transitions and bugs):
   - nvim_render_all_tabs: render_all(), then iterate each tab in order, capturing a snapshot per tab. Tests that images don't bleed across tabs (the ghost image bug lcarcat-2m7.9).
   - nvim_tab_sequence TABS: navigate through a list of tab indices, sleeping and snapshotting each. Useful for verifying TabEnter re-render fires correctly on each transition.
   - nvim_split_then_render: open a vsplit, render in one pane, switch panes, verify images don't appear in wrong pane.

These should live in test/nvim_harness_helpers.sh and be sourced by scenario scripts:
  source "$REPO/test/nvim_harness_helpers.sh"

Design question: should the helpers take the kitty socket and window ID as arguments, or read them from environment variables (LCARCAT_TEST_SOCK, WIN)? Env vars are simpler for scenarios that already export them; args are more composable for multi-window scenarios.

title: nvim: periwinkle gutter continues to EOW and merges with statusline elbow
description:
## Goal

The gutter (line-number column) should remain periwinkle (#9999ff) all the way to the bottom of the nvim window, even when the file has fewer lines than the window height. Currently the gutter goes black below the last line of content.

At the bottom of the gutter, the periwinkle stem should merge into the statusline via an LCARS elbow swoop — the same style as the top-left corner chrome.

## Confirmed root cause

nvim 0.12.2 does **not** evaluate the `statuscolumn` expression for EOB (below-end-of-buffer) virtual rows. Confirmed empirically: setting `statuscolumn=%#LineNr#%{v:virtnum}` shows the value on real lines but the cells for EOB rows remain blank/black — the expression is never called.

`winhighlight=EndOfBuffer:SignColumn` does paint the gutter periwinkle on EOB rows but bleeds the color across the full row width (text area included). Not usable.

statuscol.nvim was evaluated and also cannot fix this — its per-segment `hl` wrapping depends on the same `statuscolumn` evaluation path that nvim skips for EOB rows.

## Design: floating window fill

A `style="minimal"` floating window positioned over exactly the EOB gutter cells:

```lua
nvim_open_win(buf, false, {
  relative = "win",
  row      = wi.botline,      -- first row below last line of content
  col      = 0,
  width    = wi.textoff,      -- exact gutter column count
  height   = wi.height - wi.botline,
  style    = "minimal",
  focusable = false,
})
-- then:  vim.wo[win].winhighlight = "Normal:SignColumn"
```

Confirmed working in the test harness: col 0–3 periwinkle on all EOB rows, col 4+ (text area) stays black.

### Events

Four autocmds, each doing one `getwininfo()` call + one `nvim_win_set_config()` (or open/close):

- `BufEnter`, `WinEnter` — buffer or focus change may change botline/textoff
- `WinResized` — window height changed
- `WinScrolled` — user scrolled; botline changes

Logic per event:
```
wi = getwininfo(current_win)
eob_rows = wi.height - wi.botline
if eob_rows <= 0 → close float (file fills window)
else → resize/reposition float to correct geometry
```

The debounce pattern already used in chrome.lua applies here too.

### Integration with chrome.lua

The bottom-left elbow image already placed by chrome.lua sits at `y = statusline_row - 1`. The EOB fill float sits above that. They don't overlap as long as the file has at least one EOB row above the elbow. No coordination needed beyond existing chrome refresh.

## Cleanup required before implementation

- **Remove statuscol.nvim** from `~/.config/nvim/lua/plugins.lua` (was added directly to personal lazy config during this investigation — not from the lcarcat repo)
- **Remove `nvim/lua/lcars/statuscolumn.lua`** from the repo (the statuscol.nvim wrapper is no longer the approach)
- **Revert `nvim/colors/lcars.lua`** — restore the hand-written `statuscolumn` line (or remove it; the float approach doesn't depend on it)

## Acceptance criteria

1. Open `test/fixtures/short_file.py` in a full-height nvim window
2. `get_cell_grid.py --col 0 --expect-bg periwinkle` passes for all rows above the statusline
3. `get_cell_grid.py --col 4 --skip-rows 11 --expect-bg black` passes (text area stays black)
4. A bottom-left elbow swoop image is placed at the join of the gutter stem and statusline (existing chrome.lua behavior)

## Test

```bash
bash test/scenarios/nvim_eob_gutter.sh
```

title: Screenshot harness leaks kitty/nvim processes on scenario exit
description:
The screenshot test harness leaves processes running after a scenario finishes:

- The dedicated test kitty instance (--title=LCARCAT-TEST) survives.
- nvim command-buffer and vsplit processes inside it survive.
- The unix socket at /tmp/lcarcat-test.sock may or may not be cleaned up.

Design intent: running a scenario should be self-contained. When the scenario script exits (normally, on error, or on interrupt), no processes it launched should remain, and the socket should be gone. Currently vsplit_nvim_command_buffer.sh explicitly skips teardown 'to preserve screenshots for manual review', but the screenshots are files on disk — the live kitty and nvim processes do not need to be preserved for that. Even scenarios that do call teardown rely on kitty @ close-window succeeding on a live socket; if the harness aborts before teardown, processes leak.

Observed leftovers include nvim instances still running the command_buffer lua module hours/days after a scenario ran.

Acceptance:
- Running any scenario in test/scenarios/ leaves no LCARCAT-TEST kitty process, no nvim child of it, and no /tmp/lcarcat-test.sock after the script exits — including on error/interrupt.

title: store scenario screenshots in repo alongside scenario scripts
description:
Currently screenshots land in /tmp/lcarcat-screenshots/ and are not committed. We want a committed copy so screenshots can be reviewed in PRs and regressions are visible in git history.

Proposed layout: test/screenshots/<scenario-name>/<label>.png, mirroring test/scenarios/<scenario-name>.sh. Each scenario deposits its PNGs there instead of (or in addition to) /tmp.

Questions to resolve before implementing:
- .gitignore currently excludes PNGs or not? Check before adding screenshots to the repo.
- Should every scenario run commit its output, or only a designated 'reference run'? Committing on every run would produce noisy diffs on unrelated changes.
- Binary diff visibility: GitHub renders PNG diffs as before/after images in PRs — this is the main value. But large PNG sets could bloat the repo over time. Is git-lfs appropriate here, or are the PNGs small enough to commit directly?
- SHOT_DIR override: scenarios already respect LCARCAT_SHOT_DIR env var. Point it at test/screenshots/<scenario-name>/ and the harness writes there with no other changes needed.

Acceptance: running a scenario deposits PNGs into test/screenshots/, they are committed, and a future change that breaks a visual surface produces a visible PNG diff in the PR.

- Should it reuse one kitty instance (faster, but cross-scenario state leakage risk) or launch/teardown per scenario (slower, clean)?
- Output format: plain text pass/fail list, or structured (JSON, TAP)?
- CI integration: should this be wired to a git pre-push hook or a separate CI step?

Each scenario already installs its own launch/teardown trap. A runner that invokes them in sequence with teardown between runs is the safest starting point.

Dependency: all individual screenshot regression beads should be complete (or at least the high-priority ones) before this runner is meaningful.

title: nvim_unit.lua: headless unit test runner for frame primitives
description:
Write test/nvim_unit.lua: a headless nvim script exercising frame.lua logic — NOT a frame correctness test.

Headless can verify: row index math in append_* functions, correct line counts, correct stem-cell prefix in output lines, correct filename strings from elbow_path/corner_path, correct hl_group names passed to nvim_buf_set_extmark (read back via nvim_buf_get_extmarks).

Headless CANNOT verify: highlight group color resolution, image.nvim screen placement, visual frame correctness. Those require the kitty screenshot harness.

Test categories:
1. Geometry (pure Lua): append_header_3row appends exactly 3 lines and returns correct start row; append_footer_3row produces stub+bar+bar order; append_output_left prepends one-cell stem prefix; elbow_path/corner_path return correct filenames.
2. Annotation (headless nvim API): after annotate_stem_left, get_extmarks returns marks at every row r0..r1-1 with hl_group LcarsBlockStem; chips annotation marks carry correct hl_group names.
3. Two-pass invariant: annotate_* on empty buffer does not crash; defensive strategy (no-op vs error) documented as contract in frame.lua.

Runner: bare --headless -u NONE -l, no plenary dependency. Exit nonzero on failure.

Depends on lcarcat-non.2 (frame.lua must exist first).

title: frame.lua: extract block frame primitives from block_demo.lua
description:
Extract reusable frame-building primitives from nvim/lua/lcars/block_demo.lua into a new module nvim/lua/lcars/frame.lua. The goal is a clean three-layer API:

- append_* functions: pure Lua table manipulation, no nvim API — append rows to a shared lines table and return the start row index. These build text strings only; no highlights, no images.
- annotate_* functions: called after buf_set_lines, apply extmarks and highlight groups to a buffer. Take buf + namespace + row anchors as arguments.
- image_specs_* functions: pure path/coordinate math — return tables of {path, dx, dy, w, h} for callers to pass to image.nvim. No image.nvim calls here.

Also include: find_asset_dir (asset directory selection probing for both elbow and corner), elbow_path / corner_path / hcap_path (filename builders), setup_hls (idempotent highlight group registration).

After extraction, block_demo.lua becomes a thin orchestrator: calls frame.* in order, collects specs, writes lines, runs annotations, places images. Tab and window management stays in block_demo.

Open questions to answer before/during this session:
- Is there a case where you'd mix elbow header with corner footer (or vice versa)? What determines which to use — block height, visual style, content type?
- Should image_specs_* return specs or should they place images directly? (direct placement couples frame.lua to image.nvim; returning specs keeps it decoupled but requires callers to know image.nvim API)
- What is the right namespace strategy — one global ns per session, or one per block instance?

title: block_demo.lua: fix TabEnter ghost images and render_all() tab navigation
description:
Two known bugs in nvim/lua/lcars/block_demo.lua from the block demo session:

1. Ghost images on tab switch: windowless images are pinned to screen coordinates. Switching tabs leaves the previous tab's images visible until the new tab re-renders. TabEnter autocmd with vim.schedule(render) was added but the timing vs the next screenshot is tight — sometimes ghosts still appear. Root cause unknown: may need a longer delay, an explicit img:clear() sweep before re-render, or a different signal than TabEnter.

2. render_all() tab navigation: after rendering all tabs, the code navigates back to tab A via a bufname search. Under some conditions it lands on the wrong tab. The logic iterates nvim_list_tabpages() and looks for a buffer whose name matches 'lcars://demo/A-'. Root cause: bufname search may match a tab other than the first, or the list order is not guaranteed. Should use index 1 of nvim_list_tabpages() instead of string matching.
close_reason: Both bugs resolved informally mid-session: ghost images addressed via TabEnter vim.schedule(render) timing; render_all() tab navigation fixed to use index 1 of nvim_list_tabpages() instead of bufname string match. No separate fix session was needed.

title: Unit tests for nvim and zsh
description:
## Goal

Headless unit tests for nvim configuration and zsh prompt logic — no running kitty or display required.

## Motivation

title: Tabline: buffer label pills are flush with bar edges — should be chips
description: The nvim tabline renders buffer labels as pills (rounded-end segments), but the pills are the same height as the bar they sit in. In LCARS, pills must float with clear vertical space above and below them. When the bar is too shallow for that clearance, segments should be chips (flat rectangular segments) instead. Currently the pills look like plain rectangles because there is no floating clearance, which loses the pill identity.

description: Prototype and compare three ways to capture per-command history for the sidebar: (a) a per-window scratch file under ~/.local/kitty/tmp cleaned up on kitty quit / next launch, (b) echoing the command into scrollback, (c) fetching it from scrollback via the OSC 133 marks kitty already emits. Deliverable: a decision on which mechanism feeds the data layer, with notes on tradeoffs (persistence, robustness, cleanliness).

title: History navigation sidebar
description: An LCARS-styled side panel listing the session's past commands, letting you browse and jump to any one in the terminal's scrollback. Builds on the OSC 133 prompt marks kitty shell-integration already emits and the scroll_to_prompt binds in kitty/keybindings.snippet.conf. The prompt (zsh/prompt_lcars.zsh) already runs preexec/precmd hooks that know each command's text, start time ($_LCARS_START), exit code, and STARDATE — this epic extends that capture into a browsable, navigable history overlay.
design: Architecture sketch: (1) preexec/precmd records per-command metadata (command text, cwd, exit, duration, stardate, and the scrollback line/mark) into a per-window store. (2) A kitty overlay window (launch --type=overlay) or kitten panel renders the list in LCARS chrome. (3) Selecting an entry drives navigation in the underlying window via scroll_to_prompt / kitty @ remote control to land on that prompt's OSC 133 mark. Reuses the existing OSC 133 marks and _LC_* palette; keep everything opt-in behind $LCARS like the rest of the toolkit.
